senses: Joined together in pairs.
ety: Inflected form of conjugate. Adjective sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Konjugation, konjugieren, coined 1899 by German chemist Johannes Thiele.

senses: A horse or other animal that bucks.
One who bucks ore.
A broad-headed hammer used in bucking ore.
A stew of mutton and vegetables.
ety: Borrowed from French navarin, probably from navet (“turnip”), a traditional ingredient. However, a connection with the 1827 Battle of Navarino has been suggested. (See Wikipedia.)

senses: Covered or smeared with paint.
Having too much paint.
A Revolutionary Guard (member of the Army of the Guardians of the Islamic Revolution)
ety: From Persian پاسداران, plural of پاسدار (“guard, sentinel, watchman”), from داشتن پاس 'to keep a watch', from Middle Persian, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- and *dʰer-.

senses: A person, especially a priest or priestess, who is a practitioner in exorcism to force out evil spirits or demons from a living being.
ety: From Middle French exorciste, from Latin exorcista, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκιστής (exorkistḗs).

senses: To drive a tractor without its trailer.
To drive a truck or other vehicle without its trailer.
A report presented by Venetian ambassadors of the social conditions in foreign countries.
ety: From Italian relazione (“account, report”). Doublet of relation.

senses: An advocate of, or believer in theosophy.
The act or an instance of debarring.
A traditional horse-drawn wagon used by the Romani.
ety: Borrowed from Angloromani vardo, from Romani vordon, borrowed from Iranian (compare Ossetian уӕрдон (wærdon)), from Proto-Iranian *wart- (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wart-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, rotate”).

senses: The handle of a handgun.
The rear part of a musket, rifle or shotgun which is pressed into the shoulder.
the presence of God.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew שְׁכִינָה (shkhiná, literally “act of dwelling”).

senses: A supernatural and generally malevolent black dog in English folklore.
ety: Possibly from Middle English shucke, schucke (“demon, monster”), from Old English sċucca (“an evil spirit”).

senses: A garment resembling a dhoti, worn around the waist in Kerala, the Tulunadu region, and Maldives.
A type of bicycle hub incorporating a ratcheting mechanism, with a cassette, or set of sprockets, mounted onto a splined shaft of the hub to engage the chain.
examples: In many high-end and midrange bicycles, freehubs have replaced freewheel systems.

senses: Synonym of nanorobot.
examples: I had the nanites install the brackets, then climbed up there with the panels, placed them on the brackets, and had the nanites secure them.
Disperse into a cloud of nanites.

senses: To modify (a lock or its cylinder) to change which keys will open it.
To change the key or tenor of; to reframe.
Any device for carrying out biofiltration.
examples: Fragrant gasses such as cadaverine and putrescine are treated with a biofilter before being released.

senses: A man who uses, or is armed with, a bill or hooked axe.
examples: He is staggering as the other billmen lash their pikes at him.

senses: The quality of being sweet or pleasing to the mind; agreeableness; pleasantness
ety: From Middle English suavite, suavitee, suavyte, from Middle French suavité and its etymon Latin suāvitās.

senses: In Russia, a broad, multilane and very long straight street in urban areas, which serves as an arterial road.
ety: From Russian проспе́кт (prospékt). Doublet of prospect and prospectus.
examples: It is not a fashionable quarter, but it contains wide Prospekts, bordered by good houses, as well as some important public buildings, amongst which are the Exchange and the University.
Converging towards the central spire of the Admiralty, are the three prospekts of which mention has been made, their length being reckoned by miles.
All the streets are broad. They are classed as prospekts, oulitzi, and perouloks or cross streets, but even the perouloks would be broad streets in most of the older European towns.

senses: Able to be absorbed by a living organism.
examples: I ask him why any brand would sell a B12 supplement that isnʼt bioavailable.

senses: A set of gears, as in a car or bicycle.
The taking in by anyone of other people's livestock to graze at a certain rate.
The taking and feeding of other people's cattle in the king's forests; the price paid for such a feeding.
A charge or rate against lands.
A proponent of consumerism.
The artful use of twine to tie objects or packages.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 縛(しば)り (shibari).

senses: The act or process of eliminating segregation.
One who practises kinesiology.
The 300th anniversary of an event or happening.
ety: By surface analysis, tri- + centennial and tri- + cent- + -ennial.

senses: The way of life of a nomad or nomads.
examples: Like the Mesolithic age of 10,000-8000 B.C., the period 6000-4000 B.C. seems to be one of the fall of fortresses and the rise of pastoral nomadism.

senses: An SI/MKS unit of measure, the length of ¹⁄₁₀₀₀ of a metre. Symbol: mm
ety: From French millimètre, equivalent to milli- + metre.

senses: To stand by or near; stand around.
To beset; stand around in hostility; harass.
To surround; encompass.
To serve; be of service to; be ready to serve or aid.
ety: From Middle English bistanden, bestanden, from Old English bestandan, from Proto-West Germanic *bistandan, from Proto-Germanic *bistandaną (“to surround, support”). Equivalent to be- (“around, by”) + stand.
examples: Would not children come kindly to such out-of-door lessons, and to such practical knowledge as would always bestand them well?

senses: Word of mouth.
ety: from Middle French parole, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parable.

senses: Of, being, or pertaining to the vulva.
An oilskin hat; a southwester.
ety: Shortened from Annisquam, name of a village on the coast of Massachusetts.

senses: A conditioner product for removing tangles from hair.
A brush used for removing tangles from hair.
One who arrives; usually, one who arrives in a specified way.
examples: Mr. Kaminsky tells precisely the same story — except with Mr. Beekman as the late arriver.

senses: A type of leavened bread from northern India, made with wheat flour and usually eaten with chole.
ety: From Punjabi ਕੁਲਚਾ (kulcā), from Classical Persian کلیچه (kulīča), کلچه (kolča). Doublet of kulich.
examples: The raita is one of the best in town; goat-cheese kulcha is an unusual and tasty take on Indian bread.

senses: A lord during the Japanese feudal period.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 大(だい)名(みょう) (daimyō), from Middle Chinese 大名 (dajᴴ mjieng, “excellent one”), from 大 (“great”) + 名 (mjieng, “name”).
